# Part A: Multiple choice

## The readings

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**1.** From @Gelman2020, a good presidential election forecast combines \underline{\hspace{2cm}}

a. fundamentals, polls, and a model of how opinion changes over time
b. polls alone, each weighted by its sample size and how recent it is
c. betting markets, adjusted for the bias towards the favourite
d. fundamentals alone, since polls are too noisy until the final week

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**2.** From @Gelman2020, why is it hard to check whether election forecasts are calibrated?

a. Official results are revised for months, so forecasts cannot be scored promptly.
b. Elections are few, and state outcomes are correlated rather than independent tests.
c. Forecasters publish expected vote shares and do not publish win probabilities.
d. A probability cannot be compared with a yes or no outcome, even in principle.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**3.** From @Gelman2020, which incentive might push a forecaster to report more uncertainty than the evidence supports?

a. A confident forecast attracts more readers, which raises the forecaster's profile.
b. A wide interval scores better than a narrow one under every scoring rule.
c. A forecast that moves from day to day gives journalists more to write about.
d. A hedged forecast is rarely called wrong, which protects a reputation.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**4.** From @Gelman2020, a forecast that gives a candidate a 70 per cent chance of winning means that \underline{\hspace{2cm}}

a. about 70 per cent of recent polls show the candidate ahead
b. in situations like this one, the candidate would lose about three times in ten
c. the forecaster is 70 per cent sure that this year's polls are accurate

a. was taken with an instrument that has been calibrated recently

d. relates directly to the research question and the estimand

\needspace{7\baselineskip}

a. the value is missing for reasons unrelated to anything in the data, observed or not

c. values outside a range are not recorded at all, so those units are absent from the data
d. the same unit was measured more than once and the measurements disagree

d. It always reduces the sample below the size needed for a confidence interval.
